name: Koodalmanikyam Temple, Irinjalakuda
deity: Bharata, brother of Rama, worshipped as Koodalmanikyaswamy (Sangameshwara), a form of Vishnu
period: Attested by Chera Perumal inscriptions of the mid-9th century CE
dynasty: Chera Perumals of Mahodayapuram; later Kerala patronage
summary: Irinjalakuda's Koodalmanikyam is a rare great temple of Bharata, Rama's devoted brother — a shrine to a single deity, recorded in a Chera inscription of the 9th century and long a home of Koodiyattam.

sections.history: Koodalmanikyam is one of the very few temples in India dedicated to Bharata, the brother who ruled Ayodhya in Rama's name with Rama's sandals upon the throne. Its antiquity is firmly attested: a stone inscription of the Chera Perumal king Sthanu Ravi Kulasekhara, dated 854–55 CE, records the grant of extensive lands to the temple, and further inscriptions of his reign survive here — evidence that the shrine was already well established by then. Over the centuries Koodalmanikyam held great estates around Irinjalakuda, and the town grew up about it. In tradition it is the second of the four Nalambalam temples, whose images the chieftain Vakkayil Kaimal installed after they were found in the sea. The temple is administered today by the Koodalmanikyam Devaswom.
sections.architecture: The temple is a broad Kerala precinct of sloping tiled and copper roofs, its sanctum standing within an unusually spacious courtyard. Inside the walls lies the Kulipini Theertham, a sacred tank whose water serves the temple's rites, and further ponds lie around the precinct. The great koothambalam, the temple theatre, is among the finest in Kerala, a tall pillared hall built for the ancient Sanskrit drama of Koodiyattam. Most striking is what is absent: Koodalmanikyam enshrines a single deity, with no subsidiary shrines at all — not even the Ganapati found in almost every Kerala temple.
sections.legends: The sthala tradition tells of the sage Kulipini and his fellow rishis, who performed a great sacrifice here; the Lord appeared, the waters of the Ganga welled up from the earth, and the sages merged into him. The Ganga, devotees believe, still dwells in the Kulipini Theertham. The temple's name comes from a later wonder. A gem was brought from the ruler of Kayamkulam to compare with the radiance glowing on the deity's image; held up beside it, the stone slipped away and merged into the idol. From this merging — koodal — of the manikyam, the jewel, the Lord came to be called Koodalmanikyam.
sections.festivals: The ten-day Utsavam in Medam (April–May) opens with the flag-hoisting on the Uthram asterism, the day after the Thrissur Pooram. Seventeen caparisoned elephants carry out the twice-daily seeveli to the beat of panchari melam, and the festival closes with the arattu, the Lord's ritual bath in a river. In Karkidakam (July–August), Nalambalam pilgrims come here second, after Triprayar. Confirm dates locally.
sections.experience: Koodalmanikyam rewards an unhurried visit. Worship here is notably austere — no lamp-waving deepa-aradhana and only three pujas a day — and the single sanctum lends the vast courtyard a rare stillness. Pause beside the Kulipini Theertham, and if the koothambalam is in use, stay for Koodiyattam, the drama that masters of the Chakyar families have performed on this stage for generations; the temple has long nurtured Kathakali and Thullal as well.

visit.timings: Open daily in the morning and the evening, with a midday closure; hours change during the Utsavam and in Karkidakam. Confirm timings locally.
visit.dressCode: Traditional Kerala temple dress applies: men wear a mundu (dhoti) and remove their shirts before entering; women wear a saree, set-mundu or churidar. Entry is generally reserved for Hindus, per Kerala custom.
visit.photography: Photography is not permitted inside the temple; the outer precinct and the town may be photographed.
visit.gettingThere: The temple stands in the centre of Irinjalakuda town in Thrissur district, about 22 km south of Thrissur. Irinjalakuda railway station, at Kallettumkara, is about 8 km east of the town, and Kochi international airport is roughly 40 km away by road.
